• Family: Cyprinidae; one of the smallest fish in the aquarium trade.
  • Size: about 1.5–2 cm in total length; up to 2.5 cm according to another description.
  • Temperature: 22–28 °C; optimal range 25–26 °C for long-term health and breeding.
  • pH 4.0–6.5, GH ≤ 5 °d, KH ≤ 2 °d, TDS < 100 ppm.
  • Difficulty: intermediate.

Difficulty: intermediate. They are easy to keep once the aquarium is stable, but due to their small, delicate nature and their need for soft water to really thrive, they are not recommended for beginners. Be sure to have the habitat ready before purchase.
Malaysia, Indonesia (Sumatra) and south-east Thailand. The Sumatran form is found in southern and eastern Sumatra, Indonesia.

A tiny, vividly coloured blackwater species found in peat-swamp forests and forest-edge streams. These habitats are shaded by dense forest canopy, with dark, tannin-rich water, minimal current, and heavy accumulations of decaying leaves and branches. In this environment B. maculatus displays intense copper-orange to red hues and a distinct dark lateral spot, creating beautiful contrast against the blackwater background.
Prefer a densely planted aquarium with plenty of hiding places, such as rocks and driftwood. Keep in groups of at least 10–12 individuals.

Soft, highly acidic blackwater is essential to replicate its native peat-swamp habitat.

  • pH 4.0–6.5 (another description: 4.5–6.5; prefers pH as low as 4.5)
  • GH ≤ 5 °d
  • KH ≤ 2 °d
  • TDS < 100 ppm (another description: 0–60)
  • Temperature: 22–28 °C (72–82 °F); optimal range 25–26 °C for long-term health and breeding

Provide slow or still water with leaf litter, driftwood, and fine plants. Subdued lighting and a dark substrate will deepen body coloration and reduce stress.

Micropredator: in the wild it feeds on small aquatic crustaceans, insect larvae, zooplankton, small invertebrates and insects. In captivity, offer finely crushed flakes, high-quality micro-pellets, and live or frozen foods such as baby brine shrimp, cyclops, microworms and daphnia. Multiple small feedings per day are ideal.

Exceptionally peaceful; best kept in a species-only or nano community setting with other tiny, gentle fish. Excellent companions include Boraras brigittae, Sundadanio axelrodi, Pseudomugil luminatus, or small Caridina shrimp, as well as other blackwater fish such as licorice gouramis (Parosphromenus) or small mouthbrooding bettas like Betta channoides and Betta albimarginata. Avoid large or active species that may outcompete them for food.

Schooling behaviour enhances both colour and confidence; keep in groups of at least 10–12 (another description: 6–8). They thrive in low light, with blackwater conditions and botanical cover. Though small, they are energetic swimmers that display best in open midwater space surrounded by dense vegetation, spending most of their time in the middle and upper levels.
The body is elongated with a golden or yellow colour. A distinctive pattern of dark spots along the sides and a red or orange stripe on the fins.

An open-water egg scatterer; breeding can be difficult in captivity. Spawning occurs among fine plants, moss (such as Java moss), or leaf litter. Use very soft, acidic water and subdued light. Adults may eat eggs; remove the eggs after spawning. Eggs hatch within 36–48 hours, and fry become free-swimming after 3–4 days. Feed infusoria (động vật nguyên sinh) or liquid fry food at first, then transition to baby brine shrimp as they grow.
